body_markdown:
Mission Log, November: ServiceNow, Linear, Azure Boards and Audit Logs now in Escape


*Escape findings now open as ServiceNow incidents and Linear issues that sync both ways. And every action that people take in Escape is kept on record for 15 months, filtered by person, action, and date, pulled into a SIEM by API or CLI.*


Until a finding actually gets fixed, a pentesting program is a known exposure sitting in a report that’s buried in a backlog. So what ultimately matters is the time between knowing your exposure and remediating it, because that’s where your risk of cyber attacks really lies.


Across five years of pentest data in a 2026 State of Pentesting report, only 52% of findings were ever found to be resolved. In the same survey, 57% of executives said their teams meet remediation SLAs, but only 15% of practitioners agreed.


It’s clear the gap is hard to show upward. And that doesn’t just lie between executives and practitioners. 41% of 650 CISOs said they couldn’t connect ROI to their risk mitigation and remediation efforts.


That leaves two divides: one between finding an issue and fixing it, and one between doing the fix work and proving the effect it had for the company.


This release narrows both of those gaps, shortening the find-to-fix window and giving you a record you can stand behind:


1. **ServiceNow integration:** findings open as incidents, with request evidence attached and status synced both ways
2. **Linear integration:** findings open as Linear issues, mapped to each team's own workflow states
3. **Azure Boards integration:** findings open as work items in your Azure DevOps projects, with request evidence attached and status synced both ways
4. **Audit logs:** a 15-month record of what people did in Escape, filterable in the app and pullable by API or CLI


ServiceNow, Linear, and Azure Boards join our existing[Jira](https://escape.tech/blog/from-alert-to-action-escapes-jira-integration-explained/) integration. All of them run through Escape workflows, so you decide which findings go where.


## ServiceNow: findings become incidents, and stay in sync


In many large organizations, ServiceNow is where infrastructure work gets tracked, and the app teams live somewhere else. When a pentest finding lands on an internal service or a shared platform, its owner may never open Jira.


[Escape now creates a ServiceNow incident from a finding](https://docs.escape.tech/documentation/automate/notifications-ticketing/servicenow/#servicenow-to-escape) , through a workflow you define. Fire it on every new issue that matches your conditions (say, a high-severity finding on an externally exposed asset), or push a single issue from its Ticketing tab.


An Escape finding linked to its ServiceNow incident


Each incident carries the issue name, context, and remediation, with a link back to Escape. The HTTP requests and responses behind the finding are attached as JSON files.


Severity then sets the incident's impact and urgency, so a Critical lands at priority 1 with ServiceNow's default lookup table.


You can write any Escape property (severity, category, asset name, URL, tags, links) to any incident field in your instance, including custom` u_` fields. The rest are covered by static values, like the assignment group or the caller.


**Status syncs both ways** . Resolve an issue in Escape and the incident moves to Resolved, with a resolution code and notes filled in. Close the incident in ServiceNow and Escape marks the issue resolved on its next pull, which runs at least once a day. If both sides changed, the most recent is the one reflected. And if a later scan finds the issue again, Escape reopens the incident.


If your instance isn't reachable from the internet, Escape connects through a[Private Location](https://docs.escape.tech/documentation/platform/private-location/) . Authentication works with basic auth, an API key, or OAuth, under a dedicated` escape_integration` role you can narrow with read ACLs.


What you get:


- **Findings in the queue infra teams already watch.** Owners pick up the work in the tool they check every day.
- **One status in two places.** A fix closed in ServiceNow shows as resolved in Escape, and a regression reopens the incident.
- **Proof that travels with the ticket.** The responder sees the exact request and response without logging into Escape.


## Linear: security work in the same cycle as everything else


Product teams that run on Linear plan their week there. So a finding that’s filed in a different tracker is sat waiting until someone manually remembers to check it.


[Escape now opens Linear issues from findings](https://docs.escape.tech/documentation/automate/notifications-ticketing/linear/) , in the team you choose. Connect with OAuth and tickets come from Escape's own Linear app user, not from whoever set up the integration. A personal API key works too.


*\[Screenshot: Linear export action with team, project, and labels\]*


Each workflow picks a Linear team, plus an optional project, a parent issue to group findings under, and labels. Fixed values set the assignee, cycle, estimate, or due date. Severity maps to Linear priority, from Urgent for a Critical down to No priority for Info. Request evidence is attached as files, as it is in ServiceNow.


As with ServiceNow, status follows the issue both ways. Escape matches statuses to Linear state types rather than state names, so a team that renamed Done to Shipped needs no extra setup. Completing a Linear issue resolves the finding in Escape, and canceling it or marking it a duplicate sets the finding to Ignored. Resolving in Escape moves the Linear issue to the team's first completed state. Escape checks Linear at least once a day, and you can trigger a pull from the integration page. The latest change wins, and a sync never triggers another one, so nothing loops.


What you get:


- **Findings in the team's own cycle.** Security fixes get planned right next to everything else.
- **Your workflow as it is.** Renamed states, labels, and projects continue working.
- **Tickets that outlive any one account.** With OAuth, tickets belong to Escape's app user, so they don't depend on one employee's login.


## Azure Boards: work items for teams on Azure DevOps


[For app teams that plan in Azure DevOps](https://docs.escape.tech/documentation/automate/notifications-ticketing/azure-boards/) , findings now land as Boards work items. The Escape platform creates them in the project and work item type you pick (Bug, Issue, User Story), and optionally under a parent item.


Each work item carries the issue context, remediation, and the HTTP requests and responses behind the finding. To use the integration:


1. Map Escape properties to any Azure field, and set fixed values like area path or iteration.
2. Connect with a personal access token or Microsoft Entra, through a Private Location if your instance isn't public.


Status syncs both ways here too. When you complete a work item, Escape resolves the finding on its next pull, which runs at least once a day. If you reopen it, the finding reopens too. To send status changes from Escape back to Boards, add a workflow with the Issue Updated trigger.


## Audit logs: every action on record


If an auditor asks who marked a critical finding as a false positive last spring, or who widened the scan scope on the payments API, finding the answer should take one filter.


Escape now records what people do in the platform: sign-ins and sign-outs, scan activity, configuration changes, and changes to assets, profiles, issues, workflows, integrations, and Private Locations. Report actions and access control events (role changes, invitations, deactivations) are logged too. Each entry has a timestamp, the person's name and email, the action, the affected resource, and a readable description.


```text
[2026-11-10 14:32:18 UTC] alice@example.com | asset.updated | Updated asset 'Production API'
```


Entries are kept for 15 months. In the Organization section, you can filter by date range, person, action, target, or free text, and group by action or by person.


*\[Screenshot: Audit logs page with filters applied\]*


To keep a copy in your SIEM, pull entries from the[public API](https://docs.escape.tech/documentation/automate/public-api/) or the[Escape CLI](https://docs.escape.tech/documentation/tooling/cli/audit-logs/) on your own schedule:


```text
escape-cli     audit     list     \
--actor     alice@example.com     \
--date-from     2026-10-01T00:00:00Z     \
--date-to     2026-10-31T23:59:59Z
```


What you get:


- **Evidence you can hand over.** A filtered list replaces a folder of screenshots.
- **15 months of history in the app.** Enough to cover a full annual audit period with room to spare.
- **Your retention, in your SIEM.** Pull on a schedule and keep entries as long as your policy requires.


## What this adds up to


With this set of releases, you can take one critical finding from discovery to remediation.


For example:


1. An AI pentest finds broken access control on your payments API. Your workflow sees a Critical on an externally exposed asset and opens a priority 1 incident in the platform team's ServiceNow queue, with the request and response that prove it attached.
2. The platform team fixes it and closes the incident. On its next pull, Escape marks the finding resolved. Nobody needs to update two tools.
3. A month later, a scan finds the same issue again. Escape reopens the incident in the same queue, so the regression surfaces now instead of at next year's pentest.
4. Your auditor asks who handled it, and who marked a related finding as a false positive. The audit log answers with names and dates.


For the security team, that's hours no longer spent chasing status across tools. For leadership, it changes what you can report:


- **Status you can stand behind.** Because ServiceNow, Linear, Azure Boards and Jira sync back, open and resolved counts in Escape match what engineering actually did. The numbers you take to the board come from the system, instead of from a spreadsheet that someone rebuilt.
- **Regressions that reopen themselves.** A finding that comes back as unresolved goes straight back to its owner's queue.
- **Risk decisions with a name on them.** Every finding marked ignored or false positive traces to a person and a date, for 15 months.


Overall, that means you’re not just fixing faster, but being able to show what was fixed, when, and who decided what.


## Built for the enterprise pentesting program


Escape already fits into large organizations through SSO, roles and projects, private tenants, and Private Locations. ServiceNow, Linear, and audit logs carry that into the places where fixes get tracked and where your program gets reviewed afterward.


So findings directly reach the people who own them, their status stays true on both sides, and the record of who did what is there the moment someone asks.
